paragraphs.text: Mitochondrial myopathy with lactic acidosis is an autosomal recessive mitochondriopathy. Its cardinal features include muscle weakness, lactic acidosis and neurodegeneration, with abnormal mitochondrial ultrastructure in muscle (Saunders et al., 2015). PNPLA8-related disease covers a range of overlapping phenotypes. These include a congenital form with congenital microcephaly, early-onset epileptic encephalopathy and early death; a childhood neurodegeneration form with progressive microcephaly; and an adult-onset form with cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy (Abdel-Hamid et al., 2024). Frequent features include central hypotonia, dystonia, seizures and cerebellar atrophy (Nakamura et al., 2024).

paragraphs.text: Mastaglia et al. (1980) described a 23-year-old man with mitochondrial myopathy. Electron microscopy of muscle showed various mitochondrial abnormalities and an accumulation of neutral lipids. Histochemistry and thin-layer chromatography confirmed the lipid accumulation.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) reported a 7-year-old girl (CMH193) with a suspected mitochondrial myopathy. She had no symptoms in her first year and met her developmental milestones, although toe-walking was noted. She had a positive Gowers sign at age 2 years and could no longer walk by age 3. Her course was progressive. Features included proximal muscle weakness, dysmetria, dysarthria, a decline in fine motor skills, oral motor dystonia, and hypotonia that progressed to spasticity. She had complex partial seizures with left temporal lobe spikes on EEG. She had a very lean body habitus without weight gain and significant lactic acidosis that required bicarbonate supplementation. A quadriceps muscle biopsy at age 4 years showed variable fiber size with isolated small atrophic type 1 and type 2 fibers, and no ragged red fibers. On electron microscopy, the mitochondria showed marked disarray of the cristae and globular dense osmiophilic inclusions. There were also subsarcolemmal aggregates of abnormal mitochondria with concentric lamellar membranes, suggestive of degenerating mitochondria. Secondary lysosomes containing residual bodies were increased. Brain MRI at 33 months showed subtle bilateral increased signal in the medial globus pallidus, which was no longer seen 2 years later.

paragraphs.text: Shukla et al. (2018) also reported a girl (patient 2) of Indian/Fijian origin born to nonconsanguineous parents. She developed normally until about 13 months of age and then regressed, with epilepsia partialis continua and focal seizures. Her development then stagnated severely. She had acquired microcephaly (-4.7 SD at age 15 years), was nonverbal, and was fed by gastrostomy tube. Other features were hypotonia, proximal muscle weakness, absent reflexes, choreiform movements, dystonia and contractures. She developed progressive atrophy of the cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem, and MR spectroscopy showed a persistently elevated lipid-lactate peak. She also had hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with subaortic stenosis, abnormal visual evoked potentials, obstructive sleep apnea, elevated blood lactate and elevated GDF15.

paragraphs.text: Burnyte et al. (2023) described 2 adult Lithuanian sibs, a brother and a sister. Both had slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia and sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy beginning at age 14 years, with preserved cognition. The brother was 49 years old at the time of the report. He had lower-limb weakness, distal muscle atrophy, ataxia and gait disturbance, tetraparesis, absent lower-limb tendon reflexes, foot deformities, bilateral Babinski signs, dysmetria, and mild distal hypoesthesia. He became nonambulant at age 44 years. At age 45 he had mild dysarthria and horizontal nystagmus, his Mini-Mental State Examination score was normal, and brain MRI showed mild cerebellar atrophy. At age 21, his sister had severe axial ataxia, appendicular dysmetria, distal muscle atrophy, areflexia, and bilateral Babinski signs. EMG showed no myopathic changes.

paragraphs.text: Abdel-Hamid et al. (2024) reported 3 patients from 2 families with PNPLA8-related mitochondriopathy. Patient 1 (family I) had the congenital form of the disease. Patients 2 and 3 (family II) had progressive microcephaly, seizures beginning in infancy, progressive cortical atrophy, loss of white matter, bilateral degeneration of the basal ganglia, and cystic encephalomalacia. The authors noted that only 6 patients with biallelic PNPLA8 variants had been reported before. Those patients had a congenital form (congenital microcephaly, early-onset epileptic encephalopathy, and early death), a childhood neurodegeneration form with progressive microcephaly, or an adult-onset form with cerebellar ataxia and peripheral neuropathy.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) reported 14 individuals (6 male, 8 female) from 12 unrelated families with neurological disease and biallelic PNPLA8 variants. Many of the families were consanguineous, and they came from countries including Japan, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Turkey, Lebanon, Egypt and Iran. Age at last assessment ranged from 3 days to 33 years. Frequent features were central hypotonia (13/13), dystonia (8/12), seizures (10/14) and cerebellar atrophy (12/12). Eight patients (families 1-8) were at the severe end of the spectrum. They had congenital microcephaly (5/7), global developmental delay with no milestones attained (7/7), peripheral spasticity (7/8) and seizure onset within 7 months of age (8/8). Their neuroimaging showed a simplified gyral pattern (6/6), pontocerebellar hypoplasia (7/7) and severe progressive cerebral cortical atrophy (5/5). Four patients (families 11-12) had a relatively mild phenotype. All 4 learned to walk and then lost milestones. Three of the 4 had ataxia, 3 of the 4 had mild or no intellectual disability, and seizures were either a single event or absent. Their brain MRI showed little or no cerebral cortical volume loss but progressive cerebellar atrophy. Two further patients (families 9 and 10) were of intermediate severity.

paragraphs.text: Saunders et al. (2015) performed trio exome sequencing in a girl with mitochondrial myopathy and lactic acidosis. They found that she was compound heterozygous for 2 frameshift mutations in the PNPLA8 gene: c.334_337delAATT (p.Asn112HisfsX29) and c.1975_1976delAG (p.Leu659AlafsX4). Both mutations were confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Each was inherited from a carrier parent, and 2 healthy sibs carried neither. Neither mutation was present in the Exome Sequencing Project database or in an internal database of 1,913 samples. On Western blot analysis of the patient's muscle, the 88-, 63-, and 52-kD PNPLA8 (iPLA2-gamma) protein bands were markedly decreased compared with 3 control muscles. A 110-kD band seen in controls was also absent. Mass spectrometry identified this band as HSPA4, which the authors concluded had reacted nonspecifically with the antibody.

paragraphs.text: Nakamura et al. (2024) studied 14 individuals from 12 families by exome or genome sequencing, with Sanger segregation analysis. They identified 14 PNPLA8 variants, 12 of them novel: 4 nonsense, 5 frameshift, 3 intronic variants near exon-intron boundaries, and 2 missense variants. Every variant had a frequency below 0.001% in population databases (dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, jMorp and gnomAD). Twelve of the 14 individuals carried combinations of nonsense, frameshift and splice-site variants, suggesting loss of function. In patient 1, a Japanese patient, the intronic variant c.1625+3_1625+6del caused skipping of exons 6-8 through aberrant splicing in patient lymphoblastoid cells. The 77-kDa PNPLA8 protein was significantly reduced in the patient's fibroblasts, indicating a null effect. Patients 2 and 5 carried the splice-acceptor variants c.2075-2A-G and c.1684-2A-G, respectively. No patient cells were available, but SpliceAI predicted loss of the splice acceptor site (delta scores 0.97 and 0.93, respectively). In patient 6, a Pakistani patient with a severe phenotype, the frameshift variant p.Glu296Lysfs*6 also had a null effect on PNPLA8 protein in skin fibroblasts.
